chapters.summary: Council Member Rita Joseph introduces herself as chair and welcomes attendees to the oversight hearing on study abroad at CUNY. She describes her own study abroad experiences in the Czech Republic, Hungary, and Austria and says every CUNY student deserves similar opportunities.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph opens study abroad oversight hearing with personal story

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Rita Joseph, Chair of the Committee on Higher Education.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Welcome to today's oversight hearing on study abroad opportunities at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: CUNY legally mandates mission is to maintain and expand its commitment to academic excellence and to the provision of equal access opportunity for students, faculty, and staff from all ethnic and racial groups and from both sexes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: CUNY fulfills its mission in part by ensuring that CUNY students have access to the same breadth of experience that all college students should have access to.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That would include study abroad opportunities, which can change a student's life.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: There's really no substitute for immersing yourself in the culture of another country and gaining all of the academic and life experiences.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: that's studying outside of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Offers.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This topic is close to my heart because of my own study abroad experiences.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: As a student, I had the privilege of studying abroad in Czech Republic, Hungary, and Austria.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That experience allowed me to work at

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: the United Nations, to see politics and decision-making through a different lens.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Afterwards, I brought that experience into my own classroom as an educator, and I reminded my students they are global citizens.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Every CUNY student deserves the chance to discover that for themselves.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph says research shows study abroad builds leadership and 21st-century skills, improves on-time graduation, and especially benefits underrepresented minority and need-based students. She quotes researchers on equity and compares access for community college students to students at Harvard.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph cites research on graduation and equity benefits of study abroad

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The research shows that students who study abroad develop leadership skills and 21st century skills.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Often sought by employers.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The research also shows that students who study abroad are more likely to graduate on time and further that students from underrepresented minority groups on a need basis aid the most from studying abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Donald Rubin, co-author of one research study, commented, if we are concerned with equity in higher education and completing college,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Helping these students study abroad seems efficient.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I believe that we are concerned with that at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Looking specifically at community college data shows that under 2% of U.S.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Study abroad students were studying an associate degree, from Susan Laventure, former director of international education at Community College in North Carolina, remark.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If we want to be equitable, our students should have the same access to study abroad as students at Harvard.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This is what I want for our community college students at CUNY.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph says the committee wants to know how CUNY advertises study abroad, whether students can afford it, and who enrolls. She notes interest in CUNY's summer and fall programs and in plans to sustain and expand them.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph frames committee questions on awareness, cost, and expansion

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Today, the committee is interested in how CUNY study abroad programs are advertised so that as many CUNY students as possible are made aware of them.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And whether a substantial number of CUNY students can afford to participate in them, and how

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: many CUNY students from what background enrolls in the programs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The committee is looking forward to CUNY's discussion for their summer study abroad program, which had just finished, and their fall program, which had just started.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Finally, the committee is interested in CUNY's plan for sustaining and expanding these programs.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Now I want to acknowledge

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Areola on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I also would like to thank Giovanni Piquant, my chief of staff, Ben Atkinson, my director of policy and budget,

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Amita Kalawan, the committee's senior legislative counsel, Regina Paul, the committee's senior legislative policy analysis, and Ali Stouffer, the committee's financial analysis.

chapters.summary: Kim Holland, University Director of Global Education and Initiatives, thanks the committee and introduces Stephen Ferst of the College of Staten Island and Jessica Rothman of Hunter College. She frames study abroad as part of CUNY's mission to provide affordable public education and says the programs often represent students' first experience away from home.
chapters.title: Kim Holland introduces CUNY global education team and mission

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: All right, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Is that better?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairperson Joseph and members of the City Council Higher Education Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today about study abroad at CUNY Colleges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I'm Kim Holland, University Director of Global Education and Initiatives in CUNY's Office of Academic Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I am joined today by my colleagues Stephen First, Executive Director of the Center for Global Engagement at the College of Staten Island, and Jessica Rothman, Professor of Anthropology at Hunter College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: The trends I will describe reflect the work of staff, faculty, and administrators who are committed to study abroad as part of CUNY's mission of providing a first-rate, affordable public education to all students, regardless of means or background.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Their commitment is based on the disproportionate impact that study abroad has on Q.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: CUNY students for whom these programs often represent their first experience away from home or even outside of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Stephen First will provide the perspective of a campus that offers 32 programs in 17 countries and which last year sent 151 undergraduate students from 12 CUNY colleges abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Jessica Rothman will describe how she has used her networks and access as an honorary wildlife officer at the Uganda Wildlife Authority to create research, fieldwork, and credit-bearing opportunities for CUNY students.

chapters.summary: Holland presents data from fall 2025 through summer 2026: 1,512 undergraduates from 15 campuses studied abroad in 49 countries. She notes 89.1% used CUNY-sponsored programs, most participated in winter or summer sessions, and 28% were community college students.
chapters.title: Kim Holland reports 1,512 CUNY undergraduates studied abroad in 49 countries

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: The following data are based on activity at CUNY's 11 four-year campuses and seven community colleges from fall 2025 through summer 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: During this period, 1,512 CUNY undergraduates from 15 campuses studied abroad in 49 countries.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: 89.1% of these students participated in a program sponsored by a CUNY campus, while 10.9% participated in an independent program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: 24.4% of CUNY students who studied abroad participated in a program for one or two semesters, and 75.9% participated in winter and summer intercession programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: 72% of these were students at our four-year campuses, and 28% studied abroad while enrolled at a community college.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: During this period, 10 CUNY campuses offered 136 programs in 40 countries, all of which were operated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Each CUNY campus may develop programs that align with its respective curricula, institutional relationships, and faculty available for in-house program development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Where appropriate, campuses are encouraged to open their programs to students from other CUNY campuses, and last year, 16.9% of CUNY students who studied abroad did so using ePermit,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: CUNY's mechanism for cross-campus registration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: This collaboration among CUNY campuses substantially broadens the scope of programs available to students, not only in terms of geographic location, but also in terms of curricular focus and available terms.

chapters.summary: Holland describes CUNY-sponsored programs as exchange, faculty-led, and affiliated. She explains how faculty-led and affiliated programs are financed through tuition and fees, while exchanges let students pay home-campus tuition and often rely on scholarships or Gilman funding for Pell-eligible students.
chapters.title: Kim Holland explains CUNY study abroad program types and funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: CUNY-sponsored programs are structured in three different ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: As student exchange programs, as faculty-led programs, and as affiliated programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: These three program types are based on their cost structure and on whether academic content is delivered by external institutions or by CUNY faculty who travel abroad with students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Faculty-led programs are designed and taught by CUNY faculty in the summer and winter intersessions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: CUNY faculty led 25 programs in 16 countries last year on topics ranging from architecture in Spain to

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Zen Meditation in Taiwan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Affiliated programs are established when a CUNY college enters into an agreement with a third-party provider or foreign university.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: These programs contribute to the breadth of CUNY's offerings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Faculty-led and affiliated programs are financed with CUNY tuition, typically supplemented by a program fee that covers expenses that exceed the cost of tuition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Exchange programs are based on partnerships between a CUNY college and a foreign university and allow participants on both sides to pay tuition only at their home institution while studying at the partner university.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: In addition to processing eligible financial aid, several campuses issue scholarship awards to their students for study abroad, and some campuses subsidize the cost of specific programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Campuses also actively promote external funding opportunities, in particular, the Benjamin A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Gilman Scholarship Program, which focuses its resources on Pell-eligible students for study abroad.

chapters.summary: Holland thanks the committee and argues that study abroad gives CUNY students judgment, adaptability, and emotional intelligence employers seek. She says it prepares graduates to compete in New York City's economy and turns to Stephen Ferst for a campus perspective.
chapters.title: Kim Holland closes testimony on study abroad and workforce readiness

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: In closing, I would like to thank the committee for its interest in this important topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: At a moment when AI and related technologies are reshaping labor markets, graduates applying for their first professional jobs are having to demonstrate judgment, adaptability, and emotional intelligence at the very beginning of their careers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Study Abroad equips CUNY students with the professional maturity that employers are now demanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: demanding of their most junior hires, and in so doing, prepares them to compete in and contribute to the economy of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: My co-presenters will provide further context on how study abroad as a high-impact practice, like internships and other forms of experiential learning,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: make a profound difference in the academic and professional trajectories of CUNY students and graduates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That concludes my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I turn now to Stephen First to share his perspective from the College of Staten Island.

chapters.summary: Stephen Ferst, Executive Director of the Center for Global Engagement at the College of Staten Island, says study abroad is integrated with international recruitment, programming, and faculty development. He says CUNY's 136 programs aim to offer every student in every major an overseas opportunity.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst describes study abroad as part of CUNY's academic fabric

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: As Kim Holland mentioned, my name is Stephen First and I am the Executive Director of the Center for Global Engagement at the College of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: In this role, I coordinate the overall internationalization and our strategy at the college to oversee our efforts of studying abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Bringing in international students, our on-campus international programming, our faculty development, our scholars, and our international intensive English language program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I mention these specifically as I want to highlight that study abroad sits squarely in the academic enterprise, does not exist in a vacuum, but it is part and parcel of the academic fabric at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: As you might have gained from their previous testimony, the experiences we offer are varied in nature and appeal to a broad range of students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: This is by design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: With CUNY's 136 programs, we endeavor to offer every student in every major an opportunity to study overseas during their academic career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: This is central to our mission, and we hold these values not just because we understand the value of enhancing a student's worldview, but also because we understand the benefits of studying abroad for all students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: For example, students who study abroad have a 95.1% six-year graduation rate, a full 30 points higher than their peers who stay at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They're also 6.2% more likely to graduate in just four years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: For first-generation students, that number goes up to 11.6%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They graduate with higher GPAs, 52% go on to graduate degrees, and they earn 6.3% more, that's over $4,000, in their first job, and find that first job sooner than graduates who do not study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: These hold true across the nation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Succinctly put, study abroad is good for the student, it's good for CUNY, and it's good for New York City.

chapters.summary: Ferst identifies time, family and work obligations, curricular constraints, and finances as barriers. He highlights the Asia Pacific University program in Beppu, Japan, where students pay CUNY tuition, receive financial aid, and study on a bilingual campus with students from many countries.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst details barriers and the Japan APU exchange program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Of course, study abroad is not without barriers to participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Many of our students find that time constraints grounded in family and work obligations, curricular strengths that leave little room for electives, and of course financial barriers that burden their opportunity to study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: At CUNY, we work every day to help students overcome these barriers, and our programming often demonstrates that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: As an example, one of our programs at Asia Pacific University in Beppu, Japan, is a program that combines flexibility of academic programming, lower costs, and strong international student support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: APU is a special type of university in that it was founded based on the principle that it would serve all students, mainly from across the Pacific Rim, but also from across the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: To do so, they pledge to offer 100% of their courses in both Japanese and in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: The students come together on one campus to learn from their professors and from each other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's a true blending of cultures that forms its own unique.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: environment and when visiting the campus our students see and hear the diversity of the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: In the cafeteria they're likely to hear at least 50 languages being spoken around them as students mingle from over 890 countries and they do so as exchange students paying CUNY tuition and often receiving significant financial aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Making this program one of the most affordable around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: This is but one example of CUNY's global programs that cater directly to our students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And while CUNY has developed a wide range of opportunities to serve the broadest range of students, those barriers I mentioned earlier can keep our students from studying abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: My colleagues and I work to lower these barriers every day through counseling and advisement by developing a wide range of program formats, especially shorter summer and winter programs, and by working in concert with our faculty and deans on academic alignment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Through the coordination of financial aid and other scholarships for study abroad,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We also help our students obtain every dollar of financial aid that they are entitled to, ever mindful of our mostly non-residential students, many of whom live at home with their families and face now a steeper constraint in living expenses when studying abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And while Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Holland mentioned the overall numbers of students studying abroad each year, I wanted to also bring to your attention the ways in which that number

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: obscures perhaps the true work done by our offices across CUNY for our students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Yes, 1,500 CUNY students study abroad each year, which also means that 1,500 students have just returned whose grades

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Records, transcripts, and accounts must be updated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: 1,500 students are preparing to go abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They need guidance on academics and finance, travel, and cultural adjustment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And yet there's likely to be another 3,000 students who go abroad who will unfortunately never have the means to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So in short, CUNY study abroad professionals are working with over 7,500 students each year, preparing, advising, processing, and assisting in their dreams to study abroad.

chapters.summary: Ferst tells the story of Catherine Yena, who studied in Greece and went on to become a Watson Fellow, Fulbright recipient, and Peace Corps member. He says expanding access to study abroad is key to CUNY's mission and describes students as global citizens.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst shares student success story and closing appeal

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And if I may indulge the committee for just one additional moment, I want to tell the story of one amazing woman, Catherine Yena, who studied abroad in Greece.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I had the pleasure of teaching Katie in my class as well as sending her abroad, which she describes in her own words as, of all my time in college, studying abroad has definitely been the most memorable and educational experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Going out into the world and learning about another culture firsthand will teach you far more than what you learn in a classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Katie's experience abroad helped her become a Watson Fellow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: She won a Fulbright to Tunisia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: She's now been accepted into the Peace Corps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Truly a remarkable woman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So those lucky CUNY students, the few like Katie, they have this life-changing experience that we often describe as the single most impactful experience of their undergraduate career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We believe the work in expanding access to these opportunities is key to CUNY's mission of providing a first-rate, affordable public education to all students, regardless of means or background.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And we believe that our students...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Our students who have these opportunities are redefining what New Yorkers can and should expect from an education at the largest public urban university in the most cosmopolitan city in the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: As we see it, we're shaping lives for decades to come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're creating global citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We are bringing CUNY to the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I sincerely thank you for your time and for your attention today.

chapters.summary: Jessica Rothman, professor of anthropology at Hunter College, says she grew up in the Bronx and studied wild gorillas in Uganda as an undergraduate. She now leads CUNY programs in Uganda, including a winter course and summer research, with 89 CUNY students participating to date.
chapters.title: Jessica Rothman introduces Uganda wildlife study abroad programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I'm Jessica Rothman, professor of anthropology at Hunter College, where I've been a faculty member since 2008.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And my research is based in Uganda and focuses on the nutrition and ecology of wildlife, including apes, monkeys, giraffe and rhinos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And I'm a lifelong New York City resident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So I grew up in the Bronx near the Bronx Zoo and the New York Botanical Gardens, and I frequently visited the wild animals and plants within them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And as an undergraduate, I had an amazing opportunity to assist a graduate student in Uganda through a study abroad research experience where I studied wild gorillas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: This is as an undergraduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: That experience changed the entire course of my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: When I joined Hunter College as faculty, I wanted to bring similar opportunities to CUNY students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I'm here to highlight my study abroad programs where CUNY students study wildlife and conservation in Uganda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: There are two kinds of programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: The first is a winter program where students take a class in January.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: and receive course credit towards their degree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: The second consists of summer research where students work alongside me and my Ugandan colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: These programs vary between two and eight weeks, depending on the particular trip.

chapters.summary: Rothman explains that students observe wild monkeys and apes, record behavior data, identify trees, use GPS, and learn from Ugandan wildlife practitioners. She says students eat meals with faculty and Ugandan experts, participate in a naming ceremony, and receive orientations on culture, wildlife safety, and expectations.
chapters.title: Jessica Rothman describes Uganda research training and cultural immersion

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: To date, 89 CUNY students, including 57 undergraduates, have participated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And I'm not alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: My CUNY faculty colleagues lead study abroad programs and include students in their international research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Students learn to conduct animal behavior research by observing wild monkeys and apes like chimpanzees, gorillas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: They record, analyze data, identify individual animals, and document whether they're feeding, resting, traveling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: They learn to identify trees and measure their growth and use GPS units to navigate through the dense rainforest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: They work in teams with me, other students, and Ugandan colleagues engaging directly with the scientific method.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: They learn about the challenges of wildlife management from field lectures by Ugandan practitioners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: For example, students visit a savannah national park filled with elephants, buffalo, and lions, and learn about poaching threats as well as human-wildlife conflict.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Our long-term collaborations with Ugandan experts and communities are an essential part of these programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: The students eat many of their meals with me and the Ugandan experts they learn from, and this is often the first time they've interacted on this level with faculty and scientists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: They don't use...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: usually have these opportunities at commuter colleges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Just before their departure, the students participate in a cultural ceremony where a village elder gives them a local Ugandan name.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Students develop profound connections with one another and the Ugandans they've met.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: The impact of international experiences on CUNY undergraduate students is immense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Students learn about opportunities in several ways beyond campus advertisements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So I talk to students who ask me questions in classes or do well on exams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Alumni visit classrooms to speak about their experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Students could not imagine that they could be following wild monkeys and apes as part of their degree program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And when they hear other students speak about their experiences and see their photos, they're very excited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: No prior experience is necessary, but we conduct interviews to make sure that the student is comfortable being away from their family, is prepared to walk in a forest all day, and is willing to have limited phone and internet time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: To prepare, the students are required to attend a three-hour orientation with me in which I cover cultural norms, training on how to behave around wildlife, and the expectations and responsibilities while abroad.

chapters.summary: Rothman says winter program students often self-pay with aid, while summer researchers are funded by National Science Foundation grants that have supported 22 students with funds for 16 more. She highlights alumni who pursued PhDs, fellowships, and careers in science and public service.
chapters.title: Jessica Rothman outlines funding and alumni outcomes from Uganda programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: They also receive a general pre-departure orientation from Hunter's Office of Education Abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: For the Study Abroad Winter Session program, many of the students self-pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Some can offset these costs with applicable financial aid or scholarship funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: The majority of the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: The students who accompany me for summer research are funded by National Science Foundation grant monies from the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: We have funded 22 students in this way and still have funds for 16 more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: In closing, I will highlight a few student impacts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Kandra Cruz-Cabreros was an undergraduate human biology major who was a Sikh student and the first in her family to attend college.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: After traveling to Uganda in 2019, she applied for and received a very competitive graduate fellowship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: She's now a PhD candidate in anthropology at NYU and soon to complete her studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Natalia Grube was an undergraduate anthropology major who came to Uganda not once, but twice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: She then completed a master's degree at Hunter in Anthropology and moved on to complete a Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: In Anthropology at Penn State University.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Now she's a genomic biologist at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease in Washington, D.C.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Camille Stewart was an undergraduate geography and anthropology major who also studied in Uganda twice during her undergrad degree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: She then completed a master's degree at Columbia University and is now a scientist at the New York City Department of Environmental Protection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And Alyssa Smith was a first-generation women and gender studies major who traveled to Uganda a year ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: She wanted to learn more and received a prestigious language area fellowship to study Swahili in Tanzania.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And she just arrived back to New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Now she's applying for a Fulbright fellowship to return to Uganda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: aims to study international environmental law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: These students demonstrate that the impact of study abroad doesn't end when the plane lands back at JFK.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: For many, these experiences open doors to graduate education, scientific research, public service, future international work, and careers they just may have never imagined before having the opportunity to go abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And then we try to use the information that the student gave us to, you know, to make suggestions for them and to help craft their resume, to put it on their resume, to identify the skills they learned while they were abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: We also take, we also put study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: opportunities specific that our human biology students might be interested in on our website.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And they also do get something when they enroll in the major, they get a little, you know, they get just information about what study abroad programs can actually contribute to their degree program, as well as, you know, just being a study abroad program, but also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: they can gain credit for actually doing that program within their degree program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So I think it's been really helpful for their, you know, in connecting them to future careers, whether it be in the city or just, you know, or outside in the future.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph says CUNY should explore international internships and mentorships with New York City companies that have global footprints. She says students who studied in a particular country develop cultural knowledge and empathy that could support future partnerships.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph suggests international internships with NYC companies

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Yeah, I was going to ask about the possibility for international internships, mentorships.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Right here in the city, too, we have a lot of companies that have footprints in international countries that maybe we should be thinking about.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Future partnerships right here and the fact that that student studied in that particular country has the norms and and it also develop empathy skills right when you learn about other cultures you're supposed to have that

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: different set set of skills of empathy towards so that's great so thank you

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph cites research that study abroad students are more likely to graduate on time and with higher GPAs, asking how important active recruitment is. Stephen Ferst says students are not running to the door and describes a national drop-off from 80% interest in high school to 6-7% participation in college.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks how CUNY recruits more students to study abroad

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: A research study showed that study abroad students were 6% more likely to graduate in four years.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And four percentage point more likely to graduate in six years than their peers who did not study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And further, that study abroad students graduated with a higher GPA.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If these findings are generally true for U.S.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: College students, how important is it to

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: CUNY to make an active effort to recruit more students to study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are these findings true for CUNY or you don't have an issue?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Everybody's running to your door to go study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They are not running to our door.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: How do we get them there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We recruit very, very broadly to get the largest number of students to study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We know this is a high-impact practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We know that studying abroad is good for these students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Allen has a bit more of the statistics on how many of our students do study abroad and some of those other impacts and where we follow national trends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I can tell you anecdotally, we do follow those national trends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Nationally, when you ask a high school student if they'd like to study abroad in college, you will get about 80% of the students raising their hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: When you ask if they expect to, you will get about 50% of the students raising their hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: When you ask them when they graduate college, if they did, you will get 6% to 7% of the students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: The drop-off is tremendous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And it is on us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It is on all of us educators to build this into the curricula, to build room for this, to put this into major advising, and to show students that it's possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: At CUNY, we try really hard to do that by showing the examples of students who have gone before, by fundraising outside, by working on exchange programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We have a lot of exchange programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: One of our campuses deals with almost 60.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: exclusively exchange programs and sends hundreds of students abroad that way, allowing students to pay that same CUNY rate at home as they would abroad, and that as they would if they stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And that has been a tremendous boon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Another campus has partnered with an external organization to give scholarships directly to their students, and that also has raised the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: CUNY needs to, each of our colleges need to create these partnerships to find ways to make it most affordable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That is probably the number one barrier for our students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And behind that is probably our academic barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We can work to lower those somewhat easier, actually, by talking to our departments around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: But one other thing that works is simply by changing the culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Simply by showing students that it is possible, by showing students that, oh, your peers have gone, everybody's going, you should go too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And although that does require the students then to sometimes find those funds, it's amazing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: When they realize this is something important, when they realize this is something that helps their life move forward, helps their academic career and their professional career, they find the way.

chapters.summary: Holland says CUNY created a consolidated study abroad directory to help students find programs available by e-permit. She says the directory is necessary but insufficient because students need a campus culture where they see peers studying abroad and feel they have the right to participate.
chapters.title: Kim Holland explains CUNY study abroad directory and campus culture barriers

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We have to find a way to keep the 80% hands up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Chairperson, just to add something to this, I think there's a measure that we took probably about 12 years ago, which we previously had each college had its study abroad page.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And even though some campuses are very generous in opening their programs to students throughout CUNY, it wasn't effectively available because it required those students to hunt through all of those websites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So we now do have a consolidated directory, which, among other things, allows students to focus on programs that are available by e-permit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Now, I will say I was really proud of this step forward.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And now I realize how insufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It's necessary, but it's not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And here's why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It goes to a mindset issue, which is the student level factor that is alongside culture at the campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Faculty can talk about it, but if students don't see their peers on their campus studying abroad, if you can't jumpstart that,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It's going to be extremely difficult, even if you have programs available through a different CUNY campus, even if you can pay CUNY tuition and get your CUNY financial aid, you're going to be effectively

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: pioneer in your space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So students we do know are very much tied to the culture of their campuses and we do have some campuses where we need to do more to support just the beginnings of that culture and so that students understand themselves

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: as really having the right to participate in these experiences and that they they're equally relevant for them as well.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph suggests recruiting returning students as credible messengers and ambassadors because students listen to peers. Ferst recalls a CSI anti-litter campaign with student posters and says CUNY could copy that model to show New York City students taking on the world.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph proposes student ambassadors; Stephen Ferst recalls campus campaign

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So maybe you need to recruit some of the students who went abroad and become that credible messenger for you, become that ambassador and tell their stories.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Students like to listen to each other.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: No matter how great we are as educators, they're like, yeah, all right, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But if a peer says, hey, I had such an amazing time in this experience, you should go.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: These are the things that I did.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This is the path that I took.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: They'll listen to their peers over us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Might I add that when I arrived at CSI, which was about 13 years ago, there was a campaign that had just concluded or was just concluding where the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: college, I believe, had partnered with, definitely with the city, to create a grant program to create posters of students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And it was a clean up the campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It was a non, it was don't trash the campus campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And there were little quotes from all these students, leaders across campus saying, this is what I say about trash.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And this is what our mascot says about trash and why you shouldn't litter on campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And I remember that this campaign, as I think about it, was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: is both a kind of a partnership between the college and between the city to develop these.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So it was pretty effective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Students were able to see themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Students were able to see other student leaders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And we would like to copy that type of campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And I think that's a collaborative thing that we could do across the city, show New York City students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Taking on the world.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We should, and that's one of the things I've always encouraged New York City public schools to do, get the students involved.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Let them be the voice.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Empower them as they, as I said, just like peer tutoring.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I can teach something very well and students don't take it, but another peer comes in and it's easier.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph cites an almost 8 percentage point graduation-rate difference for underrepresented minority study abroad students. Holland says last year's participants were 34.2% Hispanic, 11.7% Black, 4.5% multiracial, 27.4% white, and 22% Asian, and that 48.7% were Pell eligible but only 1.2% had public assistance history.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about underrepresented minority participation; Kim Holland gives data

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Research studies show that underrepresented minority students, the difference in graduation rate in six years was almost 8% percentage point for study abroad students compared to those who did not study.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If the findings are generally true, how important is the community to make an active effort to recruit students to study abroad?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are these findings true?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: For underrepresented minority students to study abroad?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do we recruit?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I have a few statistics on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So last year, 34.2% of our students who studied abroad identified as Hispanic, 11.7% identified as Black, and 4.5% identified as multiracial.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: White and Asian students made up 27.4% and 22% of our study abroad students, respectively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Now, we know that that is not well aligned with our overall populations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So 48.7% of our students who study abroad are Pell eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And unfortunately, at the very low end of the income spectrum, we see that only 1.2% of our study abroad students are or have at some point in their college career qualified for public assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That's based on CUNY Edge data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So we can follow up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We're still getting support from our institutional research team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I'd love to provide a little more on first-generation students, which is another angle to look at it through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But I think all of this says we are making some progress here, but it is woefully insufficient, and we're very conscious of that fact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I also really appreciated that you highlighted in your opening remarks that community college students should be studying abroad more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Our statistics bear that out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We do, in fact, have one community college that has been extremely successful with support from an outside organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But that's not a solution for each of our community colleges, and we need to create space for all of them to find.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Their own solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I do want to say I had hoped, and I'm still trying to parse through the data, I had hoped to find more

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: more evidence of students who transfer from community colleges studying abroad after they transfer as vertical transfer students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So far, the patterns I've found have not been encouraging, but I think that that specific population, targeting those students,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: identifying the barriers that face our vertical transfer students would go a long way towards the access and equity priorities.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks whether barriers for underrepresented students are financial, fear, or lack of information. Rothman says extra mentoring is needed and notes her Uganda programs have largely matched Hunter's underrepresented student population, including the four alumni she highlighted.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks how to encourage underrepresented students; Jessica Rothman responds

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do we get our underrepresented students to want to take that leap of faith to say, I want to study abroad?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do we create that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What are some of the barriers we see?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is it financial?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is it just a fear?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is it because they just don't know?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: In some cases, it requires a little bit of extra mentoring and reaching out to those specific students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: when they express an interest to identify barriers to participation, whether it be their family, whether it be financial, whether it be they're worried about their academics, to see where we can help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And I think that faculty and advisors can do a good job of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I also wanted to mention that the four cases that I mentioned, the four students I mentioned in my testimony are all underrepresented minorities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And my program actually seems to represent the student body at Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: which is 70% is about, about 70% is our underrepresented students of color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And that seems to be what my programs have, have been in the past.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So, so I, you know, I feel happy that we've been able to attract students that wouldn't traditionally go on study abroad.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks whether campuses share best practices for recruiting underrepresented students. Ferst says education abroad liaisons meet monthly, then notes that study abroad historically served mostly white, upper-middle-income women and that moving the needle on diversity remains difficult nationally.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about sharing best practices; Stephen Ferst discusses field history

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Copying the model, are you talking to each other to see what are some of the best practices that maybe we can transfer to other campuses for it to work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We have a monthly liaison meeting of folks who work in education abroad, study abroad, and we do try to bring those best practices across campus to campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I will say this is my 37th year in this field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I have been working on, the field has been working on underrepresented students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: For that entirety of the time, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: When study abroad started in 1966, 1967, those first students went abroad on those.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They were young women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They were studying languages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They took a boat to France.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They spent a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They came home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Until the 1980s, when we really massified or diversified studying abroad, that's who went abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And it remains still mostly women studying abroad, mostly white women who are upper middle income and above.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: These barriers exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They've been extremely hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: to move the needle on students of color, on students of limited means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: There are a number of programs out there, 100,000 Strong in the Americas is a grant program, the Gilman program, and several others that I know all of us at CUNY have worked very hard to achieve those grants to overcome these things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I think CUNY does better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: The national, honestly, in overcoming these barriers for first underrepresented students, but this is a needle that is extremely hard to move nationally.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: After recognizing Council Members Dinowitz, Brewer, and Epstein, Chair Joseph asks about top study abroad countries. Holland says Italy leads since 2013, followed by Spain, Japan, China, France, England, South Korea, Germany, Greece, and Australia, with Spain tripling and China dropping 78%.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks top destinations; Kim Holland cites Italy, Spain, Japan, and China trends

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize Councilmember, we've been joined by Councilmember Dynowitz, Brewer, and Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What are some of the top countries that you visit?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That's an excellent question, and we've seen some interesting changes over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Overall, if you look at trends since 2013, you see in first place, no surprise, Italy, followed by Spain, Japan, China, France, England, South Korea,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Germany, Greece, and Australia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I don't think that this will come as any surprise to anybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But what is interesting is that we are also seeing trends where Spain is almost tripled during this period.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Italy is down by 23%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That may reflect a decrease in the number of families that are first and second generation Italians.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But we do still have a very robust CUNY Italy program that supports exchanges throughout our system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Followed by Japan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Japan has gone up 2.4 times in participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Participation in England is 2.4 times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: South Korea is up 5.3 times, which...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Really astonish me, but I think if you look at the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: cultural surge of South Korea, I may be a little less surprised.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And we also have a couple of professors who lead very interesting programs on media studies in particular in South Korea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: This is very compelling for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And China is down 78%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Now,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I don't think that that is necessarily a permanent trend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We did see, obviously, through the pandemic and policies that impacted both Chinese citizens and visitors some trepidation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But Stephen First can speak to, you know, a campus that is rebuilding in that area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But at some campuses, they have chosen to focus on Taiwan, for example, for their students who want opportunities to learn Chinese language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So those trends tell you a little bit about what students are trending towards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But what I really like about our programs is that there's a huge breadth available and that the students are always encouraged not just to think about the locations they're going to, but about the academic focus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And to really look at this as not just...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: tourism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It's a very different experience than they will have even five years after they graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They will be able to participate in their host countries in an extremely different way.

chapters.summary: Ferst says CUNY's top destinations differ from national trends, where the UK, Italy, Spain, and France have long dominated. He says CUNY has purposefully created programs reflecting its students' diversity rather than replicating decades-old destinations.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst contrasts CUNY destination trends with national patterns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I'll add here again that CUNY bests the nation, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So nationwide, the top destination is England, the UK.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Then you've got Italy, then you've got Spain, then you've got France.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Those are the top four.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They've been the top four for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: To hear the statistics where those are not CUNYs, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: These are things that we've purposefully done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: How do we provide something different for our CUNY students?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: How do we create programs that reflect the diversity of our CUNY students as opposed to doing what's been done for decades?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Going to England, going to Italy, going to Spain, going to France.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We actually do far better than the rest of the nation in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That's something that CUNY can be proud of.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks about emerging countries and mentions Uganda. Jessica Rothman cites Morocco, and Ferst describes a CUNY-wide medical internship in Morocco where students do observational hospital rounds in obstetrics, oncology, pediatrics, and pharmacy, shaping their career decisions.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about emerging destinations; Stephen Ferst describes Morocco medical internship

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And what are some of the emerging countries that you see students are interested in now?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know Uganda's one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: We see Morocco, actually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: There's a very popular CSI program in Morocco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: That students are interested in.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm going to chaperone the one to Morocco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's actually developed for CUNYwide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It is a medical internship program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So students spend four weeks in Morocco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They get up every morning very early.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: You might want to rethink the chaperoning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And they go on rounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They go on rounds in a hospital with doctors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's an observational program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They make their rounds through obstetrics, through...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Oncology through pediatrics, through pharmacy, and each day they go to maybe three or four sessions of different rounds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: They spend time in the OR, and they really learn quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I have two quick stories about two students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: One who I visited when she was there, and she had just come out of the OR room, and she showed me her hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: She goes, look at how steady I am.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I was born to be a surgeon, and this program just cemented what I want to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And another student who came back and said,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Thank you for sending me on this program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I never want to step foot in a hospital again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So we were able to, with two students, really set the trajectory of their career with this program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It is very popular across CUNY, and it gives students an experience that they just can't get anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's why I'm championing this.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer says private high schools offer abroad programs and asks whether CUNY has a central grant for study abroad. She asks how funding is assembled from foreign governments, U.S. sources, New York, philanthropy, and foundations.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer asks how CUNY funds study abroad opportunities

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Dynowitz, question?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's so important.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Even the private high schools have abroad programs now because I was with some students and they're off to wherever, South Africa in this case.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, how do you go about the funding?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I teach at Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I see all the signs up.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You can go here.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You can go there on the bulletin boards.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But I worry who's going to be able to go here and there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, is there a central CUNY grant for these kinds of opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I remember years ago, I have to say the Eisenhowers and the Bushes and so on, some of the more conservative heritage type have funding that I know some of the public school students have taken advantage of in the past.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It doesn't exist now and it won't exist for another three years probably.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, how do you go about the funding and what can we do in that sphere?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because this doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Either it's foreign government's pain, it's U.S.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Pain, it's New York, it's somebody.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Philanthropy, foundations, how do you go about getting that funding?

chapters.summary: Holland welcomes advice on funding and says CUNY can identify which students are missing out. She says many students express interest but back away when they realize the cost, and CUNY needs to increase the share who actually depart.
chapters.title: Kim Holland says CUNY needs resources to target students who back away

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So we would welcome any advice in that realm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And we do think that there is a compelling case to be made for specifically for CUNY students to have these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: This is something that we think that we could also really specify which CUNY students are not getting these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And, you know, as we're all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
