utterances.text: Underscoring again and again, study abroad changes lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And that's critical, but we also have to ask ourselves whose lives are being changed and who is expressing interest but having to back away because they realize the reality

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: of financing these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And so Stephen first described the vast numbers of students that come into his office and only a fraction of them actually wind up crossing that finish line and leaving from JFK.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But how can we make, how can we increase the success rate by telling these students that we have resources for them?

chapters.summary: Brewer recalls her work under Mayor Dinkins, when city agencies applied for federal money and secured $90 million in six months. She asks who at CUNY is responsible for pursuing every possible dollar, including conservative foundations interested in international experience.
chapters.title: Brewer urges CUNY to apply for every possible federal and private grant

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: When I've worked for David Dinkins, I was head of the federal office and I made every single city agency apply for federal money.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We got $90 million in the first six months.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If you don't apply, you don't get.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So, and they had never applied.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I guess my question is, what's CUNY doing?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because this is the kind of thing that even the more conservative foundations are interested in.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So it's not like a political thing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's a we need to improve America in their head by giving people international experience, blah, blah, blah.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I guess my question is who at CUNY is taking that we need to apply for every single possible dollar on this front.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're not going to do other things, these foundations, that CUNY might want to do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's my question.

chapters.summary: Rothman says faculty can include students in international research grants, which has funded 22 students with support for 16 more. She warns that federal grants are rapidly depleting.
chapters.title: Jessica Rothman says faculty research grants fund students but are depleting

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I mean, I was just going to speak from I'm a faculty member at Hunter and I could speak from the faculty experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: We get research grants and we can include students in our research grant, international research for students in our research grants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And there are specific grants from the federal government that are international experiences for for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: You know, that's been something that I've had a lot of success with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So, you know, in my testimony, I.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I list it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I don't remember how much here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: 22 students so far, and then we still have funds for 16 more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: But those grants are going away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So the grants in the federal government are just rapidly depleting, unfortunately.

chapters.summary: Brewer says federal help is unlikely now but private foundations remain interested and CUNY must apply. She tells CUNY to focus on pursuing those opportunities.
chapters.title: Brewer stresses private foundations and focused grant-seeking

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I said three years.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was very clear.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But there are still private foundations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm just saying you have to be like focus, focus, focus.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The feds are not going to help right now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The private foundations, this is something they would be interested in, but you have to apply.

chapters.summary: Ferst says study abroad offices share grant opportunities, use CUNY tools, and pursue programs like 100,000 Strong and Gilman. He says the federal government rescinded $69.4 million overnight, and CUNY is working to get that money back.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst describes grant efforts and $69.4 million federal rescission

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We are, those of us who run study abroad, the study abroad offices, we do talk about what grants are out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We do use the various.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: as tools that CUNY has supplied to find grants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I can, you know, there's 100,000 Strong is one campaign that's North and South America.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: The ideas, which came out of the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: State Department, is still going.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And obviously through NSF grants, through

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: private grant, I'm sorry, through programs like the Gilman for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We do work every day to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I think I've applied for five of those grants this past year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And yes, those are specifically designed to lower the cost and to allow our CUNY students to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I will say as of last night, the federal government rescinded some of that money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That makes it easier for me to do my job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That was $69.4 million gone overnight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're working on getting that back.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: But we do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We lobby for that money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I go to Washington and work for that money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And we certainly apply for as many grants as possible to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's not easy.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, it's not, but that is the only way to do it at this point.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Eric Dinowitz, a Hunter alum, asks whether CUNY has a goal for study abroad enrollment as a percentage or number. Kim Holland says CUNY wants growth but has no specific target, including within programs like SEEK or ASAP.
chapters.title: Council Member Dinowitz asks about CUNY study abroad enrollment goals

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Councilmember Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Hello, CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm wearing my hunter purple today as a hunter alum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is CUNY's goal for study abroad enrollment, for example, an intended percentage of total student body or enrollment figure?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So that is, that's an excellent question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think that we have overall goals of growth, but overall growth alone would not be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We really look at how the participation is going to break down in terms of our students who are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: traditionally underfunded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We do see some positive trends in the past when programs such as SEEK and CD and ASAP and ACE have funded their students to study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We know that there is potential there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But we also know that just as we see with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: advisement patterns where those students in those programs have lower advisement ratios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We have a vast population of students who are not under the umbrella of any special program, and we need to find ways to reach them as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So your general goal is growth?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But you don't have a specific target, even within those specific programs, like within the SEEK program or the ASAP program, we will increase by a certain percentage or a certain number of students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Those goals don't exist?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what groups CUNY wants to reach. Holland identifies vertical transfer students as a major target and says they face mindset and academic integration barriers, including fewer electives and difficulty fitting study abroad into degree plans.
chapters.title: Dinowitz presses for target populations; Holland cites vertical transfer students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: At this point, no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That would have to be a conversation with each of those programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I would like to see a higher participation of the underrepresented groups, and I think through that we are going to...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are those?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you give an example of what those groups are?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think by our vertical transfer students are a major group, and that's something that we can target directly by looking at the obstacles those students face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: In addition to the mindset,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: obstacles that these students often face.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We also see them having a greater barrier when it comes to academic integration of these opportunities because they tend to have fewer electives available and that does make it harder to study abroad when you have less room in your schedule.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So we need to offer programs that have more courses that fit into their degree plans.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So it sounds like you have

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The concept of a plan for a goal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But it also sounds like you do actually have like a target population where setting a goal

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: would actually be helpful, even in the raising, you know, the money element as Councilmember Brewer was referencing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so you asked for ideas besides asking the council for money, which we always love to give CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think setting goals for particular populations lends itself to a better sales pitch for other outside funding or even government funding.

chapters.summary: Ferst says many campuses have goals and notes CSI aims for 10% of graduates to have a substantial international experience. Dinowitz says concrete goals like 10% would help engage students and make stronger funding pitches.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst cites CSI's 10% study abroad goal; Dinowitz supports targets

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I can add that I think many of our campuses have goals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So I represent the College of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I'm the director there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And we do have a 10% of the– we have a goal that 10% of the students who walk across our graduation stage at our ceremony will have had a substantial international experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That would place us–

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: squarely in the top quartile of public education, right, of students who study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now we've got to get the other colleges to compete with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Well, so we've got Hunter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That's doing great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We've got a number of other colleges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: What we will say is that the senior colleges that benefit from programs like the Macaulay Honors Program and other schools tend to have higher percentages because of some of those programs and because of those student populations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: But yes, those are goals, and I think that that would be shared by my colleagues across campuses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Around 10%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Again, placing us near the top.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would share that I think having specific goals like 10% or increasing those goals year after year would be

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: a step forward, I think, in engaging more students in the study abroad program, which is widely recognized as being a positive experience.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Whether it gets you to be a surgeon or it tells you, gets you not to be a surgeon.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes calls to boycott relationships with Israel and asks whether CUNY intends to cease relationships or reduce programs. He asks whether the number of Israel programs has remained the same or increased over four years.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks about CUNY programs and relationships with Israel

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, my other question is about, you know, there have been numerous calls to, I don't know, numerous, but there have been calls to boycott all relationship with the nation of Israel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The chancellor has spoken out against this, I think, very forcefully in the past.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to confirm that it is not the intention of CUNY to cease relationships, that the relationships, the number of programs students have opportunity with to Israel has not decreased,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: have the number of programs remained the same.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or increased over the past four years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Okay, that's an important question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I'm glad that you asked it.

chapters.summary: Holland says CUNY reviews programs for safety and does not approve unsafe travel. She says a multi-institution Israel exchange program was sunset before current events due to lack of reciprocal demand, rebuilding efforts are paused, and students can still study in Israel independently with a travel warning waiver.
chapters.title: Kim Holland explains Israel program sunset, safety review, and independent study

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So first, before we address that, I just want to say that CUNY does not approve travel anywhere where we can't prepare our students to travel safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So we review every program and we monitor conditions continuously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: CUNY did used to have a program in Israel that was with a number of Israeli institutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And that was sunset.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: There was a sunsetting process that happened well prior to current events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That led to this type of pressure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It was really much more about the difficulties in balancing the exchanges with those institutions because Israeli students had less demand to come to CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: The way it was explained to me is that many Israeli students are older when they start their university careers, and they are much less likely to fit study abroad into what they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Now, we know that many Israeli students do wind up at many very high-profile institutions, but we've had a hard time making sustainable exchanges work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Now, we have had some efforts to rebuild that that were interrupted since October 7th.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But those are merely on pause.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They are not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And in the meantime, as you know, we have many students who have, from the beginning, you know, since they were in elementary school, they were told someday you will spend at least part of your time as a college student in Israel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And those students have used our option to study abroad on an independent basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They do have to go through an additional step of the travel warning waiver petition, which goes through Central.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We issue a recommendation, and the campus provost makes a final decision.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So CUNY students have continued to go to Israel for study abroad, even through this interlude, which we hope is temporary.

chapters.summary: Ferst says around 2018 CSI developed agreements with four Israeli universities, some offering up to $6,000 per semester scholarships. The agreements were interrupted by the pandemic and then the war, but he maintains relationships and says CSI is ready to resume when safe.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst details paused CSI agreements with Israeli universities

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And if I'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So circa 2018 or so, CSI was aggressive in picking up the pieces of opportunities for students to study in Israel, beginning

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: conversations and agreements with four Israeli universities to ensure that students had broad access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Some of those institutions were actually going to give significant scholarships to CUNY students upwards of $6,000 a semester to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That was interrupted first by the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Then we went back on track to start our agreements again, and yet then interrupted again by the war that is currently happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And so because of the State Department warning levels, because of the safety regulations,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We have had those on pause.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I will say I continue to maintain those relationships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I myself studied at Haifa University in Israel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I go back to all of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We talk about when we're going to be ready.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We have everything ready to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We have all of our marketing material ready to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We have all of our agreements ready to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: When it's safe for us to send students, we will.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Absolutely be resuming sending students to Israel through CUNY.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks to be kept informed on numbers and outreach for Israel programs. He says travel abroad, especially to a fellow democracy, has value during polarized times and says he will follow up with CUNY.
chapters.title: Dinowitz requests updates and stresses exchange value with Israel

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, I would like to be kept abreast of the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the progress in that outreach, I mean, independent of everything else,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: traveling abroad has value, especially to Israel, a fellow democracy, but particularly at a time of such polarity in our country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, the exchange of ideas and knowledge is of particular importance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So this is...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, an issue I want to continue to see, ensure CUNY does not go on the downward slope, that it does increase.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will certainly be following up and would appreciate the response and the outreach back from CUNY as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph thanks Dinowitz and asks how CUNY can fund study abroad through private-public partnerships. Rothman says departments and faculty have pursued outside funders and small private grants, but these efforts vary by campus and depend on individual faculty and chairs.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about public-private funding; Jessica Rothman describes departmental grants

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Dinowitz.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Earlier, just to piggyback off of Councilmember Brewer, we know that cost is a big obstacle for students.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Are we thinking, how do CUNY help students come abroad, and how do we find money elsewhere, probably private-public partnerships to make this happen?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So any thoughts on that?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I mean, I can speak to the, from the perspective of being a faculty member and just from my own department, is that we have engaged outside funders and private small grants for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: But these are on a campus and sometimes departmental basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And it also depends on the efforts of individual faculty, individual department chairs, individual, you know, campuses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So, but we have, you know, taken advantage of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Of those funding opportunities when they come across.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph calls the CUNY study abroad search engine a great tool and asks how many students use it and how success is measured. Holland says usage data is limited because there is no login requirement, but e-permit participation is an important indicator.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about usage of CUNY study abroad search engine

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The CUNY Study Abroad search engine looks like a great tool for students to use and find study abroad opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many students use it and how do you gather data on it?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how do you judge whether it's successful or not?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think we could do a better job at looking at usage rates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It's a little difficult because we are all in such a concentrated space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So using data about where the users are is not going to show us necessarily which campuses they're from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We did not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We made a conscious decision not to create sort of a login requirement so we could see exactly who was there, although that would have given us really granular data we could have followed up on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But I think the 16.9% of students who are studying abroad on e-permit is an important indicator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And another indicator I would really like to see grow is the number of campuses that are taking, where students are taking advantage of e-permit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Because we know we have campuses that don't currently have the staffing to support their own programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But that does not mean that those students shouldn't have the opportunities to study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And there are opportunities, but as I mentioned,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: If there is not a culture on the campus where students see peers taking advantage of those opportunities, you have a really tough time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: reaching just a sense where students feel like this is something that they should be investigating for themselves.

chapters.summary: Ferst says CSI and Hunter use application software that tracks student progress and a 43% melt between phases. He also describes a sophisticated transfer credit system being rolled out to show students exactly how overseas courses count back at CUNY.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst describes tracking software and transfer credit tool

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: To add to that, we do use a software that runs our application system at the College of Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Hunter has also purchased that software.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: After we went through the purchasing process, we were able to help other campuses go through it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So we do share among campuses those experiences and are trying to expand that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That does track students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That does track usage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That's how we know that 43% melt between one phase and another phase might happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So that is one other way that then we can go back and target why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Why are we seeing that melt?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: What are these particular students dropping off for, and how do we address that in particular?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Another of our campuses have developed a very sophisticated transfer credit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: System so that a student can look at a course overseas and see exactly what it's going to count for back at CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And it builds itself every time a new student does a new program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That is being rolled out across, I think in about six weeks, going to be presented to all the other campuses to be rolled out perhaps to all the campuses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So any student throughout the entire system will be able to, similar to the T-Rex system if you're familiar with that, that's a transfer internally mostly in CUNY, this would allow our students to know what they can take abroad and exactly what it's going to count for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So we do start to share systems that try to lower those barriers.

chapters.summary: After Chair Joseph recognizes Council Member Wilson, Council Member Harvey Epstein asks for data on household income of study abroad participants. Holland says 48.7% are Pell eligible but only 1.2% have qualified for public assistance, showing steep barriers at the lowest income levels.
chapters.title: Council Member Epstein asks about income breakdown of study abroad participants

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember Epstein, your questions?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you have data on the students who use the travel board, their household or family income, and do you break that down about lower-income students going versus higher-income students?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I have a little bit of data for you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So 48.7% of our students who study abroad are Pell eligible, and only 1.2% of our students who study abroad

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: are or have at some point during their college careers qualified for public assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So you see a big difference there in terms of financial need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Those are all students who are very low income, but at the very low end, we see very significant barriers.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks what percentage of students in ASAP or EOP receive institutional support for study abroad. Holland says ASAP and CUNY Edge have funded students, and Bronx Community College has partnered with a Salzburg institute for over two decades for a seminar embedded in a spring course.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about ASAP and EOP participation; Holland cites Salzburg program

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: How about students who are in an ASAP or an EOP program?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What percentage of the students are in a kind of program where they're getting some support from the institution?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So ASAP and also CQCD, they have provided significant funding to their students, primarily for participation in specific programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: There is a program that is primarily spearheaded by Bronx Community College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They've been working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: with an institute in Salzburg in Austria for over two decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And it brings students there to a castle for a seminar on global issues annually for a week.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They offer that now as...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Sort of a field trip within a spring semester course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So it is embedded in a broader context.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And they've made that possible for much larger numbers of students.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks specifically about semester-long study abroad for students in SEEK or ASAP. Holland says she needs to get back to him with data and agrees to examine barriers for those students.
chapters.title: Epstein asks about semester abroad for SEEK and ASAP students

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I mean, more like a semester study abroad for a student who's in a SEEK or an ASAP program.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: What percentage of those students?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I would need to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That's a really good question.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'd like to know, and I'd like to know what barriers might be for the population of students.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not arguing with you, but I just, not my, I don't want to put words in their mouths, but, you know.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then the other question is, you know, we have paid internships at CUNY now, and it's really been a benefit for a lot of the students.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: If they're doing study abroad, are there potential stipends available for students who may need financial support because of, you know, the Mayan Habana?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Ability for food and other support.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering what's available for study abroad.

chapters.summary: Holland says semester abroad may be affordable for private residential students because expenses transfer overseas. For CUNY students, however, they lose family housing, meals, and jobs that help with household expenses, so stipends would be an important resource.
chapters.title: Kim Holland explains why stipends matter for CUNY students abroad

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So I think two answers for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Just a basic answer first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: You're absolutely right that the semester abroad,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It might be very affordable for a student at a private residential institution because a lot of their expenses simply transfer to overseas, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And often their host city is much cheaper than New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: For CUNY students, they no longer can live with their parents or other family members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They're no longer eating with the family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And they also have to sacrifice that job that they are using to pitch into household expenses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So, yes, stipends would be a very important resource for those students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And Stephen can provide more texture.

chapters.summary: Ferst points to exchange programs where students pay CUNY tuition and a reopened China program under $10,000 for the semester with room, board, and tuition. He says some countries allow work authorization, which helps students afford going abroad.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst cites affordable programs and work authorization abroad

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Yeah, I can point to a few programs that we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Some of them are exchanges that allow students to pay their CUNY tuition and go abroad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: But we also have a program in China, for example, that is now reopened, that is very inexpensive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's under $10,000 for the semester, room board tuition included.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And so we work to find affordable programs specifically to allow students with less disposable income to do these types of things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's not easy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's really hard for these students to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: See themselves abroad and to give up that job, to find things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Occasionally, we are operating in countries where students are allowed to receive some work authorization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And that's also sometimes very helpful for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: In China, they cannot work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: If they do an internship, they can get lunch money and transportation back and forth, which isn't bad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And other places, you know, in Australia, for example, a student can work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: At a pretty decent rate, but it's hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's recognized it's hard.

chapters.summary: Epstein says he wants data on what percentage of students in supported programs access study abroad. He says money is a factor and wants to explore what could help targeted populations make those choices, turning back to the chair for possible conversations.
chapters.title: Epstein requests data on targeted populations and cost barriers

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I would just love to be able to see what the data says about the percentage of these students who are making these opportunities available to them because we know how important study abroad can be.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then, as the chair pointed out, money obviously is a factor, but we'd like to be able to figure out in the context of money what...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Could assist these students in making those choices?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because then I would turn back to the chair saying we maybe create some conversations around those possibilities, especially for a targeted population.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph thanks Epstein and says the committee began discussing from the start how the Council can support study abroad expansion. She says money makes things work and the Council must talk about funding.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph says Council wants to discuss funding and support

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And we started having those discussions from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How can this council support that, expand the travel, and support you?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know folks don't like to talk about money, but money makes things work, right?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we got to talk about money.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph recognizes Council Member Maloney and a Brewer follow-up. Brewer asks whether CUNY tracks Fulbright and Marshall scholars and how it prepares students for those opportunities.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer asks about Fulbright and Marshall tracking

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Councilmember, oh, at first I'd like to recognize Councilmember Maloney.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And the Councilmember Brewer has a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I know several CUNY students who've gotten Fulbrights and Marshalls.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you keep track of those, and how do you prepare?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That obviously gives you the opportunity to travel.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No kidding.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So do you keep track?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Maybe there are other similars.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Those are the two I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: My office, which is the Center for Global Engagement, oversees study abroad and other opportunities as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So we are highly engaged in working with our scholarship office, which does the primary advising for those scholarships.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We also work closely with our honors programs, both our Verrazano and Macaulay honors programs, which also is a nice...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Macaulay's in my district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Which are great feeders for those two, you know, those programs, the Fulbrights, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So we do keep track.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers of students out of one, but I will say the College of Staten Island has been aggressive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We are now in our fourth year of being a top producer, Hispanic serving institution, top producer of Fulbrights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And in 2017, we were the top producer of Fulbrights for our category of schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: So, yes, we do keep track and we put the plaques on our wall.

chapters.summary: Brewer says CSI does a great job but asks about other campuses. She says every campus needs to be more hard-hitting in applying for Fulbright, Marshall, and similar opportunities.
chapters.title: Brewer says every campus must be more aggressive on scholarships

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But what about the other campuses?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They have you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My campus does have me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Each of our campuses, I believe, does have a scholarship advisor that works closely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I don't know if they keep track with their study abroad offices.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think you're doing a great job.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I do think that every campus needs to be a little bit more hard-hitting and applying for these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think I know a lot of the students who get Fulbrights and Marshalls.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It needs to be more hard-hitting, I think.

chapters.summary: Holland says students who studied abroad are best positioned to compete for Fulbright, Marshall, and Rhodes opportunities. CUNY met with scholarship advisors to connect returning students and is sharing Gilman Scholarship information with campuses, even where no scholarship office exists.
chapters.title: Kim Holland describes connecting returning students to fellowships

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I absolutely agree, and I'm glad that you brought up Fulbright and these other opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: The way we think of Fulbright and Marshall and the Rhodes and all of these is that the students who have studied abroad as undergraduates are the best positioned to compete for these opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And so we like to connect, and we actually met last spring with the scholarships and fellowships advisors to say, how can we better connect our returning students with you so that right when they come back and they're excited

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: and they're motivated, that they know who to go to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Now, I will say some of our campuses have incredible resources in this respect and very strong track records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: There is not an equivalent point of contact to each of our institutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And so one thing that we're doing right now, because we can't magically create that equivalent resource at each campus, is for the Gilman Scholarship, which does apply for undergraduate opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We are going to share out information that our colleagues bring back from seminars with the Gilman Scholarship Administrator, the Institute for International Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We're going to share it out with all of the relevant points of contact that we can find.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And sometimes that might be a writing center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: If there isn't a scholarships office, then there are P.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: people who can support students who ask the question, but we don't want students to be told we don't do this here because we absolutely can and we should.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We all sometimes quietly needle each other to embarrass each other to do better.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Well, I think maybe we can work with a chair to do that, do better.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just put all of your, like, muse, because I'm a muse addict now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So all of your scholarships showed up and a few more.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So put it in Muse and you'll get more.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks whether all community colleges will meet to share best practices for study abroad and recruiting underrepresented students. Holland says she supports the idea but notes competitive dynamics and says leadership should come from community colleges with central support.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about community college collaboration plan

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there eventually going to be a plan where all community colleges, just the community colleges, plan to sit together to see how can we exchange ideas, better practices in having a better study abroad and recruiting?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You know, the underrepresented students that we talked about and the ones that normally would not go on that trip?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that something that we're thinking about?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I think we should bring everyone to the room and let them explain also the challenges they face in doing that work and see how we can work, all work together to make sure our students are traveling and gaining new experiences.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And all of that.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And we heard leadership skills.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm a New York City council member today.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I studied abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I was an educator.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So it paid off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think that's an excellent idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We have tried versions of that in the past.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think that the competitive dynamic that Stephen mentioned is it can be a help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: or a hindrance, and we've got to harness that correctly, because as you know, one of our community colleges has been extraordinarily successful in recent years at increasing those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think that that almost makes it look like, oh, well, you have this resource, you have a million dollars, of course you're doing well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That's not necessarily constructive, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And I do want for the leadership to come from within the community colleges and simply support it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So it's going to be tricky to find a way to accomplish this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I would like to go back and look at, you know, the college that did this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They were also a leader before they got that money, and they were providing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Fundraising for scholarships, and they didn't actually provide it as scholarships to individual students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They simply subsidized the cost of the programs that they were developing in-house, and that made it very sustainable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So, you know, whether that money is there tomorrow or two years from now really will not be decisive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They're going to be able to sustain strong programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: The question is, how can we build that up at other campuses, recognizing that they're standing in a different river.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph notes dissatisfaction with demographic participation and asks what advertising and promotion CUNY uses. Holland cites the weekly CUNY This Week email, campus outreach, and efforts to help campuses with low participation connect with neighboring study abroad fairs.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks how CUNY promotes study abroad

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay, okay, that does make sense.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know earlier you talked about how you're not satisfied with the demographic breakdown of CUNY students who study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we know we have some work to do there.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What advertising and promotion is done across CUNY campuses?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know we talked about briefly, but how else do you get word?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is it through email, advertisement, brochures?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do they find out?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And do you think it's enough?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And how come some students still are reluctant to join your program?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So I think one of the most powerful outreach mechanisms that we have right now is the weekly CUNY This Week.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: The opening rate for that is tremendous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So we've used that, and we've noticed spikes with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We need to do better with that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I've actually had conversations with one of our campuses that is in that situation that I mentioned with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Virtually no students participating.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: They are actually, they're not ready to hold their own study abroad fair, but they did ask about fairs being held at neighboring campuses, which I thought was an incredible place to start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And so we're creating those connections and figuring out good first steps to build that culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And so there are CUNY-wide efforts, but then there's also ways to support individual campuses to have messaging reach their particular populations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And especially if there aren't peers speaking to other peers, how do you build that up?

chapters.summary: Ferst says CSI uses every outlet available, including Instagram, Facebook, mailers, posters, fairs, email, EAB Navigate, and text systems. He says they aim to tell students 15 times in 10 different ways that they can study abroad, competing against commercial advertising while keeping academics central.
chapters.title: Stephen Ferst lists advertising channels and message repetition for study abroad

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: I can answer for my campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: If there's an outlet, we're using it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Instagram, Facebook, MySpace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using Muse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using, you know, we're using mailers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using posters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using fairs on campus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using email.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using EAB Navigate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We're using Rave if they let it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Let's use the text system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: You name it, we will use it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We are of the opinion, you know, the old adage was what you had to tell somebody something five times in three different ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We go for 15 in 10 different ways, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: We feel that our students need to constantly hear this message and hear it from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And hear it from day one or even before that, that they hear that they can do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And that's our message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: You can do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: One of the things that's always interesting about advertising and study abroad is you're competing against Coca-Cola and Sprite and the latest movie, and you're competing against Flash, and you're competing against things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: But you're trying to sell an academic program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: You have to sell it both as exciting and fun.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: But you have to make sure that you hold dear to the academics on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: And that makes it tricky.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: It's maybe a little bait and switch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: Get a student super interested in going to an exciting place, and then when they get there, make them study.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And they can find Coca-Cola and Sprite abroad, too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Ferst
utterances.text: That's what we say.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I hope you say that.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks whether CUNY has set a target number of students for study abroad. Holland says numeric targets are important but CUNY needs to come back with a goal and should also consider future students and whether they view CUNY as offering these opportunities.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks if CUNY has a numeric study abroad enrollment goal

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there, does CUNY has set a goal to see how many students it can enroll for study abroad?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there a number?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there a goal that you're setting?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That, hey, I want to get this particular, this amount of students to study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that something you guys are working on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: You and Councilmember Dinowitz, I think we need to come back at that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But I would like to say that although numeric targets are important, in some ways, they're always looking around the corner at the next term or two or year or two.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I really like an approach which is also informed by looking at down the road who is coming to CUNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And do they think about CUNY as a place where they're going to have these opportunities?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And to that end, I think, although it's small scale, there is something that Professor Rothman has done, which I think has planted some amazing seeds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: And I hope she can speak to that now.

chapters.summary: Rothman says her program has sent students into middle schools to talk about chimpanzees, gorillas, and study abroad experiences. She also hosts high school students in her lab and says returning students recruit peers by sharing stories and photos in classes.
chapters.title: Jessica Rothman describes middle and high school outreach for study abroad

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So we've actually gone into some middle schools to talk about the experiences that the students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: that have gone abroad have spoken in some middle schools to tell students about chimpanzees and gorillas and all the different experiences that they've had.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And the students are really thrilled about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: We also host high school students in our lab.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So they learn about the research that we do and all the opportunities that they can have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So I think that, you know, that's been really nice and also fun for me to go back to the school that I went to to show them what I've done and what they could possibly do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: But also hearing from the students who've been abroad and seeing, you know, learning from them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And I just want to, just to the earlier point, I just want to say, like,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: students that study abroad come into the classes that the students take for their life science requirement and they say

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: this summer I went and I saw a wild chimpanzee and I collected data or just this winter I went and I saw a lion and that's like all the students like what you and they show a picture I mean I think it's a really effective way of just recruiting students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: you know I'd like it if 100% of our students went studied abroad but I know that that can't be a key and goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Thanks.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks whether CUNY offers study opportunities in other U.S. states. Holland says Queens College administers a domestic study away program through a fixed set of universities using tuition reciprocity, but CUNY does not require campuses to report domestic study away data.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about domestic study away; Holland cites Queens College program

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Does CUNY offer study opportunities outside of New York City?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: other parts of the U.S., which would be considered, I guess, domestic study abroad?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there any opportunities for students to study in other states?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: There is a program administered by Queens College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: which offers this kind of domestic study away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I don't have numbers on current participation because although all of the campuses send their data on study abroad to my office, they're not required to include data on domestic study away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: But I can get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you have any examples of where they go?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Um,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It's been a while, so I don't, but it is a fixed set of universities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So it's very much based on the same model as our exchange programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So students are going to consistent institutions that are used to having our students and that we know have a good track record of taking good care of them, and that we also receive their students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So it's also based on tuition reciprocity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It's a very streamlined way for students to broaden their experience while they're undergraduates.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks if CUNY plans to expand overseas study abroad once systems improve. Holland says programs will evolve with demand and safety, citing past programs in Mali that are no longer feasible and current interest in Morocco as Middle East options shift.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph asks about expanding overseas programs; Holland discusses evolving offerings

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Once you perfect the system, because I hear that across the board that you're looking to perfect this, do you plan to expand the overseas study abroad program?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think expansion, I would say, I would like to think that the range of programs that we have is always going to evolve and respond to current opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: That will also involve some programs that...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: Either there's not enough demand or safety in that area over a period of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I will say in a previous position, I used to send students regularly to Mali.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: There were incredible opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: It was a visual and performing arts program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: You could never do that now.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: So you have to find other opportunities and grow those opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: I think that the interest now in programs in Morocco is in part a reaction to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: To problem sending students to other locations in the Middle East.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: We know that Hunter College, which has a very strong Arabic language program, has really struggled to find opportunities for its students, and they have been investigating opportunities in Morocco because their programs in Jordan

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kim Holland
utterances.text: have not been feasible for a while.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we have work to do.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph says the Council must support expanding study abroad so every New York City student can have the experience. She thanks the witnesses, says CUNY has a partner in this work, and emphasizes funding and the Muse scholarship database.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph closes with call for partnership, funding, and access

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: This council has to support in expanding.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We want to see that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know Councilman Brewer, Epstein, and Dinowitz and my colleagues, I know we talked about, one, how can we perfect this system?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How can we expand?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How can we allow every New York City student that come through your doors to experience what it's like to study abroad?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We would love to work in partnership with you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: You have a partner in this work.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know it was important for me when I did my study abroad.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And also that experience really changed the trajectory of what I wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I think CUNY has a great opportunity to do that with our students.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we have to find money, right, council member?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We need money.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Money makes everything work.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And Muse.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Music will tell us everything.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I look forward to, I'm going to reach out to you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm going to give you my email because I do.

chapters.summary: Chair Joseph asks whether Rothman does anthropology work beyond Uganda. Rothman says she travels to study monkeys and apes and colleagues work in Iceland and Madagascar. Joseph proposes a CUNY pipeline for bioanthropology and African burial ground research in New York City, and Rothman says students and CUNY anthropologists would be interested.
chapters.title: Chair Joseph proposes anthropology pipeline for African burial grounds; Rothman responds

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Any of your travel abroad do any anthropology work?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Other than Uganda, do you do anthropology work anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: I actually travel to other places, but not with students, to study monkeys and apes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: But other people in my department do additional anthropology work, specifically in Iceland and Madagascar.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: So other, you know.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: We need you here in New York.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I told you I want to create a pipeline for young students to do anthropology, bioanthropology study as we continue to discover more and more African burial grounds in the city.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I told you I have one in my district that I'm looking.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: To create a pipeline through CUNY to study more.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So mine is big.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It was there since 1600.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The city built on it twice.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It was desecrated.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So now we're looking to memorialize it, but we also want to make sure we're testing the soil, making sure we find out what was there before, similar to the one they just found in Harlem and the one in Van Cortlandt.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that the anthropology and the work, the pipeline comes from SUNY.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So I'm looking forward to talking to you and creating a partnership and a pipeline for young people to...

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: To know that this career, this field also exists.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And that was one of the things when we talked to young people, they're like, well, I didn't know that was a career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that'd be wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And I think the students would really enjoy it and they'd be just thrilled to participate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: And I know that other CUNY anthropologists would be interested for sure.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So let's have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jessica Rothman
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

summary: Committee on Higher Education holds an oversight hearing on study abroad opportunities at CUNY.
CUNY officials Kim Holland, Stephen Ferst, and Jessica Rothman testify on participation, program types, funding, barriers, and student outcomes.
Council members question enrollment goals, equity, destination trends, scholarships, and access for underrepresented and community college students.
title: Committee on Higher Education
topic: Oversight - Study Abroad Opportunities at CUNY
